source: ACIAR Monograph No. 146a, "ដំណាំសំណែកសៀង" [Soybean Growers Manual], Belfield S., Brown C., Martin M. (eds.), New South Wales Department of Primary Industries / Murdoch University / CARDI / ACIAR, 2012
text:
The manual closes with an economics chapter built around gross-margin budgeting — teaching farmers to itemize all input costs (seed, inoculant, fertilizer by nutrient, herbicide, labor for each operation, harvesting cost) against expected revenue (yield × farm-gate price) to calculate a per-hectare gross margin. Two detailed worked example budget tables are given, one for manual harvest and one for mechanized/contract harvest, itemizing costs line-by-line (seed cost, Mo and KCl fertilizer costs, planting labor, weeding labor including herbicide costs, insecticide costs, harvesting costs, threshing costs) against total revenue at a stated farm-gate price and yield, arriving at a net gross margin per hectare for each scenario — the manual's explicit point being that mechanized harvest, despite its cash cost, can improve net margin by cutting field losses and labor cost versus manual harvest, though the comparison depends on local machinery hire rates and yield levels.

A regional yield/price comparison table lists five named source areas (Ang Snuol, Kroch Chhmar, Kaeng Meakh, Kampong, Samraong Yong) with differing yield (t/ha), price (riel/kg), and resulting gross-value-per-hectare figures, illustrating that local price and yield variation materially changes which practices are profitable in a given area.
